hypotheses.title: Snuggery pet() multiplies schnibbles by 1e18 causing massive inflation
hypotheses.description: `petterSchnibbles` and `pettedSchnibbles` are computed as `((totalSchnibbles * 5) / 11) * 1e18` and `((totalSchnibbles * 6) / 11) * 1e18`. `PET_TOTAL_SCHNIBBLES` is already denominated in 1e18 (comment says 10e18/72), so multiplying by 1e18 again inflates the reward by 1e18x. Any two registered players can pet each other's snuggery NFTs to mint astronomically large `unfedSchnibbles`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker registers two accounts A and B. 2) A imports an NFT into snuggery; B imports an NFT. 3) A calls `pet(B, tokenId)` — B's player gets `pettedSchnibbles` (~1e18x too large) and A gets `petterSchnibbles` (~1e18x too large). 4) Both accounts now hold ~1e18 * real schnibbles, which can be fed to NFTs (chonks), fed to primordials, or converted via ClaimManager into MUNCH tokens.
hypotheses.impact: Unbounded schnibble inflation → free chonks, free primordial levels, free MUNCH token minting via `convertPointsToTokens`; drains token supply and breaks all downstream accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Remove the `* 1e18` multipliers: `petterSchnibbles = (totalSchnibbles * 5) / 11;` and `pettedSchnibbles = (totalSchnibbles * 6) / 11;`.

hypotheses.title: MigrationManager.rescue uses transferFrom instead of transfer
hypotheses.description: `rescue()` for ERC20 tokens calls `IERC20(_tokenContract).transferFrom(address(this), _returnAddress, _quantity)`. Since `address(this)` is the caller, this requires the contract to have approved itself, which it never does. Any ERC20 tokens sent to MigrationManager (e.g., migration lock funds held in the contract) are permanently stuck.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Users call `lockFundsForAllMigration()` which transfers ERC20 tokens into MigrationManager. 2. Admin attempts `rescue()` to recover them. 3. `transferFrom` reverts because no self-allowance exists. 4. Funds remain permanently locked in the contract.
hypotheses.impact: Permanent loss of all ERC20 migration deposits held by MigrationManager; no recovery path exists.
hypotheses.recommendation: Replace `transferFrom` with `IERC20(_tokenContract).transfer(_returnAddress, _quantity)`.

hypotheses.title: LockManager.unlock() zeroes remainder, losing dust on partial unlock
hypotheses.description: `unlock` sets `lockedToken.remainder = 0` unconditionally, even when the user only unlocks part of their balance. The remainder represents the sub-`nftCost` dust that was carried forward from previous locks; wiping it on a partial unlock silently destroys that accounting, so the next lock starts from zero remainder and the user loses the accumulated dust toward their next NFT.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User locks an amount that leaves a non-zero remainder (e.g. nftCost=100, locks 150 → remainder 50). 2) User calls `unlock(token, 1)` (partial). 3) `remainder` is reset to 0. 4) User locks again; the previous 50 dust is gone, so they need to lock more to reach the next NFT threshold.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of user dust accounting; users must over-lock to receive the same number of NFTs; unfair distribution of reveal NFTs.
hypotheses.recommendation: Only reset `remainder` when `lockedToken.quantity == 0` after the subtraction, or recompute remainder from the remaining quantity.

hypotheses.title: SnuggeryManager.pet() schnibble math multiplies by 1e18 after division
hypotheses.description: `petterSchnibbles = ((totalSchnibbles * 5) / 11) * 1e18;` and `pettedSchnibbles = ((totalSchnibbles * 6) / 11) * 1e18;` multiply by 1e18 *after* the division, whereas `PET_TOTAL_SCHNIBBLES` is already in token units (comment says `10e18 / 72`). This inflates the schnibbles credited to both petter and petted by a factor of 1e18, allowing a user to mint astronomically large `unfedSchnibbles` with a single pet call.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker registers two accounts, imports an NFT into each snuggery. 2) Attacker calls `pet` from account A on account B's NFT. 3) `pettedSchnibbles` and `petterSchnibbles` are credited at 1e18× the intended amount. 4) Attacker feeds the inflated schnibbles into `feed()` to pump NFT chonks, then claims points in ClaimManager, or converts via `convertPointsToTokens` to mint MunchToken.
hypotheses.impact: Unbounded inflation of schnibbles → inflated chonks → inflated ClaimManager points → minted MunchToken; protocol reward pool drained.
hypotheses.recommendation: Remove the `* 1e18` multipliers; keep all schnibble amounts in the same unit as `PET_TOTAL_SCHNIBBLES`.

hypotheses.title: ClaimManager._claimPoints referral bonus not deducted from claimAmount
hypotheses.description: `_referralBonus` is computed from `claimAmount` and added to `_points[player.referrer]`, but `claimAmount` is still fully credited to `_points[_player]` and `currentPeriod.claimed`. The referral bonus is therefore minted on top of the period's `available` points without being subtracted from anywhere, so total points issued per period can exceed `pointsPerPeriod + _pointsExcess`. Over many periods this inflates the point supply beyond the configured emission.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker registers account A with referrer B. 2) A accumulates chonks and calls `claimPoints` each period. 3) Each claim mints `claimAmount` to A plus `referralBonus` to B, but `currentPeriod.claimed` only increases by `claimAmount`. 4) Total points in circulation exceed the intended emission; when converted via `convertPointsToTokens`, extra MUNCH tokens are minted.
hypotheses.impact: Unbounded MUNCH token inflation; dilution of all other point holders; protocol emission cap bypassed.
hypotheses.recommendation: Subtract `_referralBonus` from `claimAmount` before crediting the player, or track referral bonuses against a separate budget.

hypotheses.title: LockManager.unlock uses unchecked ERC20 transfer, can silently fail
hypotheses.description: In `unlock()`, ERC20 tokens are returned via `token.transfer(msg.sender, _quantity)` without checking the return value (unlike `SafeERC20.safeTransferFrom` used in `_lock`). For non-reverting ERC20s that return `false` (e.g., tokens with blacklists or paused states), the state is updated (`lockedToken.quantity -= _quantity`) but the user receives nothing, permanently losing their locked tokens.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker (or any user) locks a token whose `transfer` returns `false` instead of reverting (e.g., a token that blacklists the LockManager). 2. After unlock time, calls `unlock()`. 3. State is decremented, but no tokens are sent; the user's locked balance is destroyed with no recovery path.
hypotheses.impact: Permanent loss of user locked funds; accounting desync between contract balance and recorded locked quantities.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `SafeERC20.safeTransfer` in `unlock()` and revert on failure.

hypotheses.title: unlock() leaves open ERC20 approval path and uses unsafe transfer return
hypotheses.description: `token.transfer(msg.sender, _quantity)` is called without SafeERC20 and without checking the returned bool. Non-standard ERC20s (e.g., tokens returning false on failure, or USDT-like tokens) will silently fail while state (`lockedToken.quantity -= _quantity`) has already been reduced. The user loses their locked balance but receives no tokens, and the manager retains them.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) An admin-configured token whose transfer returns false on some condition (paused/blacklisted recipient) is locked by the user. 2) User calls unlock. 3) `quantity` decremented, `transfer` returns false but is ignored, no revert. 4) User's lock balance is gone without receiving tokens; contract keeps funds.
hypotheses.impact: Permanent loss of user funds; accounting desync between `lockedToken.quantity` and actual tokens held by LockManager.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use SafeERC20.safeTransfer or require the returned bool.

hypotheses.title: Missing notPaused on RewardsManager claim functions
hypotheses.description: `claimYieldForContracts` and `claimGasFeeForContracts` are externally callable by anyone and lack any modifier (`onlyRole`, `notPaused`) that other managers enforce. An untrusted party can pass arbitrary `_contracts` addresses and force the RewardsManager to call `blastContract.claimAllYield` / `claimMaxGas` on their behalf, pulling yield/gas to the RewardsManager where it is immediately forwarded to `yieldDistributor`/`gasFeeDistributor`. While funds aren't stolen directly, this bypasses pause and role controls and can be spammed to repeatedly trigger distributor interactions.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `claimYieldForContracts([anyEOAOrContract])` in a loop. 2) Each call triggers yield claiming and distribution, ignoring the paused state and role system that other managers rely on. 3) Attacker repeats to cause gas griefing and unwanted distribution churn.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized triggering of privileged operations, bypass of the pause system, potential repeated distribution events and gas grief.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `notPaused` and an access modifier (e.g., `onlyRole(Role.ClaimYield)`) to both claim functions as originally intended.

hypotheses.title: MigrationManager allows anyone to burn anyone's NFTs
hypotheses.description: The check `if (_user != msg.sender && _userLockedAction[_user] == UserLockedChoice.NONE) revert SelfNeedsToChooseError();` only blocks third parties if the victim's `_userLockedAction[_user]` is `NONE`. If the victim has set `_userLockedAction` to any of `LOCKED_FULL_MIGRATION`, `LOCKED_BURN`, or something else, a third party can invoke `burnNFTs(victim, skip)` and the code will burn the victim's NFTs (owned by the old contract) and credit points to the victim — but the action is irreversible and consumes the victim's `_userTokenIds` entries. Because `_userLockedAction[_user]` is user-set and a single prior action makes the check pass, any subsequent caller can burn the victim's remaining NFTs without consent.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Victim sets `_userLockedAction` to `LOCKED_FULL_MIGRATION` (or performs any first burn). 2) Attacker calls `burnNFTs(victim, 0)`. 3) The condition `_user != msg.sender && _userLockedAction[_user] == NONE` is false because the victim's action is not NONE, so the call proceeds. 4) Attacker's call burns victim's old NFTs, marks them `claimed`, and irrevocably sets their choice to `LOCKED_BURN`.
hypotheses.impact: Forced irreversible state change for the victim, arbitrage of migration options, permanent loss of control over migration strategy on victim's NFTs.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `_user == msg.sender` unless msg.sender is an explicit trusted helper or remove the third-party path entirely.

hypotheses.title: MigrationManager discountFactor division by 10e12 truncates to zero
hypotheses.description: `quantity = (totalLockAmount * discountFactor) / 10e12`. If `discountFactor` is configured as a percentage-style value (e.g. 50 meaning 50%), then for typical lock amounts the result truncates to 0, and `_lockManager.lockOnBehalf` is skipped entirely — the user's migrated funds are never locked, yet their old NFTs are burned and new ones minted. Conversely if `discountFactor` is 1e12-scale, the `10e12` divisor is wrong by 10x. The same divisor is used in `migratePurchasedNFTs` and `getUserMigrateQuantityAll`, so the ETH required check and the actual lock amount can diverge.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker loads a migration snapshot with a large `lockAmount`. 2) Calls `lockFundsForAllMigration` paying `totalLockAmount` (computed with the same wrong divisor). 3) Calls `migrateAllNFTs`; `_migrateNFTs` computes `quantity` with the same divisor, so ETH is consumed but the lock amount credited to `_lockManager` is either 0 or 10x off. 4) Attacker keeps the difference or gets free NFTs without locking.
hypotheses.impact: Mismatch between ETH/tokens paid and locked amount; either free NFTs (protocol loses locked value) or user funds stuck with no lock credit.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a single, documented scale (e.g. `1e18` or `1e4` for basis points) consistently across `_migrateNFTs`, `migratePurchasedNFTs`, and `getUserMigrateQuantityAll`.

hypotheses.title: USD price proposal can be executed with stale/zero price and no freshness check
hypotheses.description: The USD price used for `getLockedWeightedValue` (which drives plot count, harvest rewards, and migration bonus) is set via a multi-sig proposal with no timestamp freshness check, no bounds check, and no zero-price rejection. Once `APPROVE_THRESHOLD` approvals are collected, `_execUSDPriceUpdate` writes `usdUpdateProposal.proposedPrice` directly into `configuredTokens[tokenContract].usdPrice` regardless of how old the proposal is or whether the price is zero. A proposal can sit unexecuted indefinitely and be executed later at an outdated price, or a zero price can be approved.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (or colluding PriceFeed role holders) proposes a price of 0 (or an extremely stale price) for a configured token. 2) Over time, enough PriceFeed role holders approve. 3) `_execUSDPriceUpdate` writes the value with no sanity check. 4) All players' `getLockedWeightedValue` collapses to 0 (or is wildly wrong), zeroing plot counts and harvest rewards, or inflating them if the price is stale-high.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong accounting of locked value → players lose plots/harvest rewards, or attacker-controlled accounts gain disproportionate plots and schnibbles; migration bonus calculations in BonusManager also use `configuredToken.usdPrice` and become wrong.
hypotheses.recommendation: Reject `_price == 0`, enforce a max staleness window on `proposedDate` at execution time, and bound the price change relative to the previous value.

hypotheses.title: AccountManager.spraySchnibblesPropose leaves stale _tempSprayPlayerCheck
hypotheses.description: `spraySchnibblesPropose` sets `_tempSprayPlayerCheck[_players[i]] = true` for each entry but never resets it to `false` after the proposal is created or executed. A subsequent proposal by the same proposer that includes any previously-used player will revert with `DuplicateSprayerError`, even though the duplicate check is only meant to apply within a single proposal.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Social role proposes a spray including player X. 2. Later, the same proposer wants to propose a new spray including player X. 3. The call reverts because `_tempSprayPlayerCheck[X]` is still `true` from the previous proposal.
hypotheses.impact: Legitimate spray proposals are permanently blocked for any player previously included; social reward distribution is DoS'd.
hypotheses.recommendation: Reset `_tempSprayPlayerCheck[_players[i]] = false` after the proposal is built, or use a per-proposal mapping keyed by proposal id.

hypotheses.title: AccountManager._harvest uses stale lastHarvestDate after registration
hypotheses.description: `register()` sets `player.lastHarvestDate = uint32(block.timestamp)`, but `_harvest` computes `secondsToClaim = block.timestamp - players[_caller].lastHarvestDate` and multiplies by `dailySchnibbles` derived from `lockManager.getLockedWeightedValue(_caller)`. A user can register, immediately lock a large amount, and then call `harvest()` — `lastHarvestDate` is the registration time, so `secondsToClaim` is small, but the weighted value is now large. Conversely, a user can register, wait a long time with zero locked value, then lock a large amount and harvest — `secondsToClaim` is huge but `dailySchnibbles` is computed from the *current* weighted value, retroactively paying the user for the entire waiting period at the new (higher) rate.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker registers an account and does nothing for 30 days. 2) Attacker locks a large amount of tokens. 3) Attacker calls `harvest()` — `secondsToClaim = 30 days`, `dailySchnibbles` is based on the new large lock. 4) Attacker receives 30 days of schnibbles at the new rate, despite having locked nothing during that period.
hypotheses.impact: Retroactive reward inflation; users can farm schnibbles for periods during which they held no locked value, draining the reward pool.
hypotheses.recommendation: On lock/unlock, call `forceHarvest` (already done in `_lock`) and reset `lastHarvestDate`; also cap `secondsToClaim` or snapshot the weighted value at the time of the last harvest.

hypotheses.title: MigrationManager rescue() uses transferFrom from self, likely reverts/fails
hypotheses.description: For ERC20 rescues the function calls `IERC20(_tokenContract).transferFrom(address(this), _returnAddress, _quantity)`. `transferFrom` spends allowance from `address(this)` — the contract must have approved itself. Unless an explicit self-approval was performed (none in the code), the call reverts or fails for tokens that require allowance. This bricks fund rescue and can strand any ERC20 that reaches this contract (e.g., WETH/USDB transferred in by lockFundsForAllMigration for locked users that never call migrateAllNFTs).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User calls lockFundsForAllMigration, transferring their USDB/WETH into MigrationManager. 2) Admin tries `rescue` after an incident. 3) rescue reverts (no self allowance), stranding user funds in an un-migratable state if seal or snapshot mismatch occurs. Additionally, any user whose unlocked migration path reverts has no fallback.
hypotheses.impact: Frozen funds in MigrationManager; users cannot recover deposits even via admin rescue path.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `IERC20(_tokenContract).transfer(_returnAddress, _quantity)` (spending from the contract's own balance) or `safeTransfer`.

hypotheses.title: getLockedWeightedValue underflows for tokens with decimals > 18
hypotheses.description: The function computes `10 ** (18 - configuredTokens[...].decimals)` with no check that `decimals <= 18`. If an admin configures a token whose `decimals` is greater than 18 (e.g., a 24-decimal token), the subtraction underflows and the call reverts. Because `getLockedWeightedValue` is called by `AccountManager.getDailySchnibbles`, `LandManager._getNumPlots`, and `BonusManager.getHarvestBonus`, a single misconfigured token bricks harvest, plot staking, and bonus calculations for every player.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not directly attacker-triggerable without admin action, but any player who locks such a token (or any player whose account is queried) causes reverts across the protocol; a griefer who gets such a token configured can DoS all harvest/plot flows.
hypotheses.impact: Protocol-wide DoS on harvest, plot staking, and bonus computation; locked funds effectively frozen for affected accounts.
hypotheses.recommendation: Revert configuration if `decimals > 18`, or normalize with `10 ** (18 - decimals)` only when `decimals <= 18` and use a separate scaling path otherwise.

hypotheses.title: getLockedWeightedValue uses usdPrice without zero/freshness guard
hypotheses.description: The function multiplies `quantity * configuredTokens[...].usdPrice` with no check that `usdPrice != 0`. If a token is configured with `usdPrice == 0` (which is the default for a newly configured token, since `configureToken` only validates `nftCost`), every player's locked value for that token is 0, so `_getNumPlots` returns 0 and `getDailySchnibbles` returns 0. Players who locked before the price was set lose all plots and harvest rewards until a price is approved.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A token is configured via `configureToken` with `nftCost != 0` but `usdPrice == 0` (default). 2) Players lock the token. 3) `getLockedWeightedValue` returns 0 for those locks. 4) Players cannot stake plots or harvest rewards; their locked funds are effectively frozen in terms of utility.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of plots and harvest rewards for all players who locked the token before a price was set; locked funds unusable.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `usdPrice != 0` in `configureToken`, or treat zero price as "not yet priced" and revert/skip rather than silently returning 0.

hypotheses.title: MunchNFT._update calls external munchadexManager before state changes
hypotheses.description: `_update` calls `munchadexManager.updateMunchadex(from, _to, _tokenId)` before calling `super._update()`. The munchadex manager then calls `nftAttributesManager.getImmutableAttributes(_tokenId)` (read) and potentially `accountManager.forceHarvest(_from)` and `accountManager.forceHarvest(_to)` (external call to AccountManager). AccountManager.forceHarvest calls `landManager.updatePlotMetadata`, which is an external call. This means during an NFT transfer (via `transferFrom`), the actual owner change in MunchNFT state has not yet occurred when external calls are made.
hypotheses.attackPath: During the mint, burn or transfer of a MunchNFT, the AccountManager and LandManager get external calls while the token ownership has not been updated. If those contracts read `ownerOf(_tokenId)`, they would see the pre-transfer owner. More critically, if any callback reentered MunchNFT's `_update`, they could transfer again with stale ownership data, though ERC721 does partial state updates before calling `_update`. Additionally the `notPaused` and no `nonReentrant` on `_update`.
hypotheses.impact: Read-only reentrancy: downstream contracts reading MunchNFT ownership during a transfer would see inconsistent state. LandManager's `farmPlots` triggered during a transfer could apply schnibbles to the wrong renter.
hypotheses.recommendation: Move the munchadex update after `super._update()` so MunchNFT state is consistent before external callbacks, or add reentrancy protection.

hypotheses.title: NFTOverlord.startReveal can be griefed via MAX_REVEAL_QUEUE
hypotheses.description: `startReveal()` increments `revealQueue[_mainAccount]` and only decrements it when the RNG proxy calls back `reveal()`. If the RNG callback never arrives (or is delayed), the queue slot is consumed. With `MAX_REVEAL_QUEUE` configured to 1, a single stuck request permanently blocks the user from starting any further reveals, and `unrevealedNFTs` cannot be converted to NFTs.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. User calls `startReveal()`, consuming the only queue slot. 2. RNG provider fails or is delayed. 3. User cannot call `startReveal()` again (`RevealQueueFullError`), and there is no admin/user path to reset `revealQueue`.
hypotheses.impact: User's unrevealed NFTs are permanently stuck; no recovery mechanism exists.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a timeout-based reset or admin function to clear stuck `revealQueue` entries.

hypotheses.title: SnuggeryManager.exportMunchable reverts if NFT was transferred out
hypotheses.description: `exportMunchable` first checks `erc721Token.ownerOf(_tokenId) != address(this)` and reverts if the NFT is not held by the contract. However, `MunchNFT._update` allows transfers out of the SnuggeryManager (only blacklist checks apply), so an NFT can be moved out of the contract while its `snuggeries[_player]` entry remains. The user can then never call `exportMunchable` successfully, and the stale entry blocks `_recalculateChonks` accounting and `getTotalChonk`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. User imports an NFT into SnuggeryManager. 2. User (or an approved operator) transfers the NFT out of the contract via `MunchNFT.transferFrom`. 3. `snuggeries[_player]` still contains the tokenId. 4. `exportMunchable` reverts on the ownerOf check, leaving the entry permanently stuck.
hypotheses.impact: Stale snuggery entries corrupt chonk accounting and permanently block export; user cannot clean up state.
hypotheses.recommendation: Reorder checks so the snuggery index is validated and removed before the ownerOf check, or handle the case where the NFT is no longer held.

hypotheses.title: RNG reveal callback lacks requestId binding, allowing replay of entropy
hypotheses.description: The reveal callback is invoked by the RNG proxy with `_player` (the revealIndex) and `_signature` (entropy). The contract only checks `revealQueue[player] > 0` and does not verify that the entropy corresponds to the specific request, nor does it bind the entropy to the requestId. Because `revealIndex` is derived from `(rngNonce << 160) | address`, and the RNG proxy stores requests by index, an attacker who can influence or observe the RNG proxy's callback (e.g., a malicious/compromised RNG proxy, or by replaying a previously used entropy) can call `reveal` with arbitrary entropy for any player that has a pending reveal, choosing the rarity/species outcome.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a pending reveal for victim (or their own) with `revealQueue[player] > 0`. 2) Attacker (or a colluding RNG proxy) calls `reveal(player, craftedEntropy)` directly on NFTOverlord, since the only check is `onlyConfiguredContract(StorageKey.RNGProxyContract)` and `revealQueue[player] != 0`. 3) The crafted entropy is fed into `_createWithEntropy`, allowing the attacker to select the desired rarity/species. 4) The revealQueue is decremented and the NFT is minted with attacker-chosen attributes.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker can mint NFTs with arbitrary rarity/species (e.g., Mythic) for themselves or others, breaking the intended randomness and economic value of the NFT collection.
hypotheses.recommendation: Bind the entropy to the specific request by including the requestId/nonce in the callback and verifying it matches the pending request; also verify the entropy was produced by the trusted RNG source.

hypotheses.title: ClaimManager._claimPoints lets late claimers drain excess from prior periods
hypotheses.description: `newPeriod()` rolls unclaimed `available - claimed` into `_pointsExcess[currentPeriodId]`, and `_claimPoints` adds `_pointsExcess[currentPeriodId]` to `currentPeriod.available` for every claimer in the new period. A user who never claimed in period N can claim in period N+1 and receive a share of the excess that was meant to compensate period-N participants. Worse, `_lastClaimPeriod[_player]` is only updated inside the `if (claimAmount > 0)` branch, so a user with zero chonk can call `claimPoints` repeatedly without ever marking the period as claimed — but the excess is still added to `availablePoints` for other claimers, and the user can later acquire chonk (e.g., via `importMunchable`) and claim the same period's excess again.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker registers with zero chonk. 2) Period N ends with large excess. 3) Attacker calls `claimPoints` — `claimAmount == 0`, so `_lastClaimPeriod` is not set inside the branch, but the trailing `_lastClaimPeriod[_player] = currentPeriodId` at the end of the function does set it. 4) Attacker imports an NFT with chonk, then in the same period calls `claimPoints` again — `_lastClaimPeriod[_player] < currentPeriodId` is false, so no double claim. However, the excess is shared among all claimers, so a user who was absent in period N still receives a share of period N's excess in period N+1, diluting the intended compensation.
hypotheses.impact: Unfair distribution of excess points; late joiners capture rewards intended for prior-period participants, diluting honest claimers.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track excess per-period and only allow players who participated in the prior period to claim it, or distribute excess to the prior period's claimers via a pull mechanism.

hypotheses.title: MigrationManager.migratePurchasedNFTs charges msg.value but ignores per-token discount
hypotheses.description: `migratePurchasedNFTs` accumulates `quantity += purchasedUnlockPrice` for each unclaimed purchased NFT, then requires `msg.value == (quantity * discountFactor) / 10e12`. However, `_migrateNFTs` internally computes `totalLockAmount += purchasedUnlockPrice` for each token and then locks `(totalLockAmount * discountFactor) / 10e12` via `_lockManager.lockOnBehalf`. If `discountFactor` is changed between the user's call and the internal lock (or if the user passes duplicate tokenIds), the ETH paid and the amount locked can diverge. More critically, `snapshot.claimed` is only set inside `_migrateNFTs`, so a user can pass the same tokenId twice in the array — the first iteration marks it claimed, the second `continue`s, but `quantity` was already incremented twice in the outer loop, so the user overpays ETH (funds stuck) or, if `discountFactor` is 0, pays nothing while still migrating.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `migratePurchasedNFTs` with `tokenIds = [id, id]`. 2) Outer loop adds `purchasedUnlockPrice` twice → `quantity = 2 * price`. 3) `_migrateNFTs` processes id once (second is `claimed`), locks `1 * price * discountFactor / 10e12`. 4) Attacker overpays ETH which is trapped in MigrationManager (only `rescue` by admin can recover). Conversely, if `discountFactor == 0`, attacker pays 0 ETH and still migrates.
hypotheses.impact: User funds trapped in contract; or free migration when discountFactor is zero; accounting mismatch between ETH paid and tokens locked.
hypotheses.recommendation: Deduplicate tokenIds before summing `quantity`, and compute the required ETH from the same `totalLockAmount` used inside `_migrateNFTs`.

hypotheses.title: PrimordialManager.feedPrimordial level loop can read unset primordialLevels
hypotheses.description: The level-up loop `while (primordialLevels[nextLevel + 1] <= chonks && primordialLevels[nextLevel + 1] > 0 && nextLevel < 1)` reads `primordialLevels[nextLevel + 1]`. When currentLevel is -3, nextLevel+1 starts at -2 (set), progresses to -1, 0, then 1 (which is unset → 0, loop exits). But `nextLevel < 1` allows nextLevel to become 1, and the final `if (primordials[_mainAccount].chonks > primordialLevels[0])` clamps at level-0 threshold. If `_reconfigure` loaded a shorter array (length != 3), primordialLevels[0..2] are 0 and the loop condition `0 <= chonks && 0 > 0` is false — so no level-up occurs, but the clamp `chonks > 0` triggers immediately, cutting user schnibbles to 0 without leveling. Also `_schnibbles -= (chonks - primordialLevels[0])` can underflow if `_schnibbles` is smaller than the clamp delta.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Admin (or misconfig path) yields empty/partial primordialLevels (allowed silently by `if (primordialLevelsTmp.length == 3)`). 2) Untrusted user feeds 1 wei and the clamp `chonks (>0) > primordialLevels[0]=0` triggers; `_schnibbles -= (chonks - 0)` may underflow → revert, locking the feed function. Even without underflow, feeding decrements unfedSchnibbles without boosting chonks proportionally.
hypotheses.impact: DoS on feedPrimordial; user loses schnibbles to clamp without leveling; underflow reverts block primordial progression.
hypotheses.recommendation: Revert `_reconfigure` if `primordialLevelsTmp.length != 3` and guard the clamp subtraction with a `chonks > primordialLevels[0]` check that only decrements by the delta actually exceeding the cap.

hypotheses.title: Primordial feedPrimordial underflows schnibbles deduction
hypotheses.description: When the player's chonks exceed `primordialLevels[0]` (the max-level threshold), the code caps chonks at the threshold and then subtracts the difference from `_schnibbles`. Because `_schnibbles` is the user-supplied amount (not the amount actually absorbed), if the user passes a `_schnibbles` smaller than `(chonks - primordialLevels[0])`, this subtraction underflows, reverting. Worse, the user can pass `_schnibbles` larger than needed which effectively wastes schnibbles (safe), but the overfeed branch also mishandles the accounting where the user paid schnibbles but only part is deducted from unfed. There is also no cap tying `_schnibbles` to what is actually consumed after capping, allowing griefing of one's own excess, but more critically the loop/level logic can be manipulated to drain schnibbles from unfed beyond what produces chonks.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Register, get approved as primordial, call `claimPrimordial()`. 2) Accumulate enough schnibbles. 3) Call `feedPrimordial` with amounts just above the level threshold; the excess branch decrements `_schnibbles` and caps chonks. 4) Repeat feeding to trigger the code path where `primordials[_mainAccount].chonks` already exceeds `primordialLevels[0]` and `_schnibbles < (chonks - primordialLevels[0])`, causing revert (DoS) or skewed level accounting.
hypotheses.impact: Player loses schnibbles or is permanently unable to feed beyond a point; incorrect unfedSchnibbles accounting leading to griefing/DoS on the primordial system.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute the absorbed amount explicitly and only subtract that from `_player.unfedSchnibbles`; avoid subtracting a delta from `_schnibbles` after capping.

hypotheses.title: BaseRNGProxy.requestRandom lacks notPaused and re-request protection
hypotheses.description: `requestRandom` is `onlyConfiguredContract(StorageKey.NFTOverlord)`, so third parties can't call it directly. However, the request mapping key is fully caller-supplied (`_index`) with no collision check — NFTOverlord writes reveal indexes derived from `(player, nonce)` and level-up indexes from a `keccak256` hash. If two distinct legitimate calls collide on the same `_index`, the second overwrites the first silently. NFTOverlord can be tricked into calling with a colliding index via the level-up path (`_requestLevelUpRng`) since the index is derived from user-controlled values (`_owner, _tokenId, _fromLevel, _toLevel`), letting a user craft a level-up request whose index equals an outstanding reveal request index and hijack the pending reveal callback (redirecting it to the level-up selector). This is triggered via untrusted external actors invoking `SnuggeryManager.feed` (which triggers level-up via `nftOverlord.munchableFed`).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker starts a reveal via `NFTOverlord.startReveal()`, causing a pending request at `revealIndex = player | nonce<<160`. 2) Attacker times a level-up (e.g., by calling `SnuggeryManager.feed`) whose `_requestLevelUpRng` hash equals the outstanding reveal index. 3) `requests[_index]` is overwritten to point at the level-up selector. 4) The next RNG callback from the RNG proxy gets delivered to `levelUp` instead of `reveal`, and the attacker's reveal never resolves, or vice versa. This effectively hijacks a pending RNG callback to a different target selector.
hypotheses.impact: RNG callback redirection: wrong function invoked with mismatched input, stuck reveal/level-up requests, DoS of reward pipeline for the affected player.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include a monotonically unique request id per call (e.g., a global counter) so collisions are impossible; and on collision, revert rather than overwrite.

hypotheses.title: addReveal lets LockManager create unbounded unrevealed NFTs
hypotheses.description: `addReveal` is restricted to the LockManager via `onlyConfiguredContract`. When LockManager calls `_lock` and `msg.sender != migrationManager`, it computes `numberNFTs` and calls `nftOverlord.addReveal(_lockRecipient, numberNFTs)`. In `_lock`, `onlyConfiguredContract(StorageKey.MigrationManager)` is only applied for `lockOnBehalf`, not `lock`. So the direct `lock` path can be used by any user to mint unrevealed NFT rights, and this call goes through unauthenticated-of-purpose logic: the recipient is `msg.sender` (or `_onBehalfOf` for `lockOnBehalf`), and the NFTOverlord trusts whatever LockManager says. That is intentional design, but `lockOnBehalf` is also callable by anyone with any `_onBehalfOf`, so a user can force unrevealed NFT entries onto another user's account via `addReveal`. Not a theft, but forced state alteration on a victim.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `lockOnBehalf(token, quantity, victim)` where `victim` is any registered main account. 2) LockManager computes `numberNFTs` and calls `nftOverlord.addReveal(victim, numberNFTs)`. 3) Victim's `unrevealedNFTs[victim]` inflates without consent.
hypotheses.impact: Unwanted/unsolicited unrevealed NFT entries assigned to a victim, potentially misleading their reveal queue accounting; forced consumption of another player's `startReveal` quota.
hypotheses.recommendation: Either remove `addReveal` when `_lockRecipient != tokenOwner` for non-migration flows, or require explicit opt-in for on-behalf locking.

hypotheses.title: LockManager._lock uses msg.sender for migration check instead of tokenOwner
hypotheses.description: Inside `_lock`, the migration bypass is gated by `if (msg.sender != address(migrationManager))`. When `lockOnBehalf` is called by MigrationManager, `msg.sender` is the MigrationManager, so the bypass works. However, `lockOnBehalf` is also callable by any user; a user calling `lockOnBehalf` directly will have `msg.sender != migrationManager`, so the NFT calculation runs — that is fine. The real issue is that `_lock` uses `msg.sender` rather than `_tokenOwner` for the migration check, so if MigrationManager ever calls `lock` (not `lockOnBehalf`) on behalf of a user, the check still passes but the `_tokenOwner` is MigrationManager, not the user. More importantly, the `remainder`/`numberNFTs` accounting is skipped for migration locks, so migrated quantities are not rounded to `nftCost` and no reveal NFTs are queued — this is intentional but means migrated users can lock arbitrary dust amounts that never convert to NFTs, and the `remainder` field is never updated for them.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker migrates a small amount via MigrationManager. 2) `_lock` is called with `msg.sender == migrationManager`, so `remainder` and `numberNFTs` are not computed. 3) `lockedToken.remainder` stays at whatever it was (possibly stale from a prior lock). 4) On the next user-initiated lock, the stale remainder is added to `_quantity`, potentially granting an extra NFT or mis-accounting dust.
hypotheses.impact: Stale remainder can be double-counted across migration and normal locks, leading to incorrect NFT reveal counts.
hypotheses.recommendation: Explicitly zero or recompute `lockedToken.remainder` in the migration branch, or gate the bypass on `_tokenOwner == address(migrationManager)`.

hypotheses.title: Migration lock amount uses stale snapshot price with no slippage/min-out
hypotheses.description: `_migrateNFTs` computes `quantity = (totalLockAmount * discountFactor) / 10e12` and then calls `_lockManager.lockOnBehalf` with that exact quantity. `totalLockAmount` comes from the snapshot loaded by `loadMigrationSnapshot` and is never re-validated against the current USD price or any minimum-out. If the USD price of the locked token changes between snapshot load and migration (via `proposeUSDPrice`/`approveUSDPrice`), the user locks a quantity that no longer reflects the intended value, and there is no slippage parameter to protect them.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a pending migration. 2) Attacker (with PriceFeed role collusion or by front-running a legitimate price update) triggers a price change. 3) Victim's `_migrateNFTs` locks the snapshot quantity at the new (worse) effective value with no minimum-out check. 4) Victim receives fewer plots/harvest rewards than expected.
hypotheses.impact: Users migrating NFTs receive locked value that does not match the intended USD amount; loss of expected plots and harvest rewards.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a `minQuantityOut` parameter to `migrateAllNFTs`/`migratePurchasedNFTs` and revert if the computed quantity falls below it; also re-derive the quantity from the current `usdPrice` at execution time.

hypotheses.title: BonusManager migration bonus uses stale usdPrice with no freshness check
hypotheses.description: `_calculateMigrationBonus` reads `configuredToken.usdPrice` from `LockManager.getConfiguredToken` and uses it to compute `migrateHighestAmount` and `halfAmount`. There is no check that the price is fresh or non-zero. If the price is stale or zero, the migration bonus is computed incorrectly (zero price → `migrateHighestAmount = 0` → `weightedValue >= 0` always true → full bonus granted to everyone; or stale-high price → bonus denied).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker waits for a stale/zero price to be set (or proposes one). 2) Attacker migrates and then harvests; `_calculateMigrationBonus` grants the full `migrationBonus` regardless of actual locked value. 3) Attacker receives inflated harvest rewards.
hypotheses.impact: Inflated harvest rewards for attackers, dilution of honest players' schnibbles; or denial of legitimate migration bonus.
hypotheses.recommendation: Reject zero prices and enforce a max staleness window before using `usdPrice` in bonus math; fall back to a safe default if stale.

hypotheses.title: MigrationManager.migrateAllNFTs can be permanently bricked by skip
hypotheses.description: `migrateAllNFTs` requires `_skip < maxSize` and processes only `SKIP_AMOUNT` (5) tokens per call. If a user's token list contains entries whose snapshots have `lockAmount == 0` (purchased NFTs mixed in), those slots are skipped but still consume the 5-slot window. A user with many purchased NFTs interleaved with locked ones can be forced to call repeatedly, and if `_skip` ever reaches `maxSize` the function reverts permanently, leaving locked funds and NFTs stuck.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. User has a mix of locked and purchased NFTs in `_userTokenIds`. 2. Each `migrateAllNFTs` call advances `_skip` by 5 but may migrate zero locked NFTs. 3. Once `_skip >= maxSize`, the function reverts with `InvalidSkipAmountError`, and the user's locked migration funds cannot be migrated.
hypotheses.impact: Locked migration funds and NFTs become permanently unmigratable; user loses access to their assets.
hypotheses.recommendation: Allow `_skip >= maxSize` to be a no-op or track a separate cursor of migrated tokens rather than a raw index.

hypotheses.title: Level-up RNG request keyed only by hash, allowing overwrite and replay
hypotheses.description: `_requestLevelUpRng` computes `levelUpIndex = keccak256(abi.encode(_owner, _tokenId, _fromLevel, _toLevel))` and stores the request in `levelUpRequests[levelUpIndex]`. If the same (owner, tokenId, fromLevel, toLevel) combination is requested again (e.g., after a failed/retriggered level-up), the previous request is silently overwritten. More importantly, the `levelUp` callback only checks `levelUpRequest.owner != address(0)` and that the current attributes match `fromLevel`; it does not verify the entropy is fresh or bound to a specific requestId. An attacker who can trigger a level-up request (e.g., via `munchableFed` from SnuggeryManager, or by feeding their own NFT) can replay a previously observed `_rng` value to force deterministic level-up outcomes.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker feeds their NFT to trigger `munchableFed` → `_requestLevelUpRng`. 2) Attacker observes the RNG proxy callback `levelUp(requestId, rng)` for any request. 3) Attacker calls `levelUp` again with the same `_requestId` and replayed `_rng` before the request is deleted, or triggers a new request with the same parameters so the index collides. 4) The replayed entropy is applied, giving deterministic attribute increases.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker can deterministically control level-up attribute gains, undermining the randomness and fairness of the game economy.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include a monotonically increasing nonce in the level-up request key and verify the callback's requestId matches the pending request; delete the request before applying entropy.

hypotheses.title: BaseRNGProxy._callback allows arbitrary target call with attacker-controlled selector
hypotheses.description: `_callback` retrieves `RequestData` for `_index` and performs `data.targetContract.call(callData)` where `callData = abi.encodeWithSelector(data.selector, _index, _rand)`. The `targetContract` and `selector` are set by `requestRandom`, which is restricted to `NFTOverlord`. However, `RNGProxySelfHosted.provideRandom` is callable by `Role.NFTOracle`, and `RNGProxyAPI3.provideRandom` is callable by the Airnode RRP. If the RNG oracle is compromised or if an attacker can influence the oracle (e.g., via a malicious Airnode), they can supply arbitrary `_rand` bytes. More importantly, the `_callback` does not verify that the target contract's function is one of the expected reveal/levelUp functions, nor does it validate the entropy. An attacker who controls the oracle role can call any function on any contract that has been registered as a target, with attacker-controlled arguments.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker gains control of the NFTOracle role (or compromises the Airnode). 2) Attacker calls `provideRandom(index, maliciousRand)` on the RNG proxy. 3) `_callback` executes `targetContract.call(selector, index, maliciousRand)`. 4) If the target contract has any function matching the selector that can be abused (e.g., `reveal` with crafted entropy), the attacker can manipulate outcomes.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker can manipulate RNG outcomes (rarity, level-up attributes) for any pending request, breaking game fairness and potentially minting high-value NFTs.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `_callback` to only call whitelisted functions on whitelisted contracts, and validate that the entropy is fresh and bound to the specific request.

hypotheses.title: LockManager.unlock() does not reset lastLockTime, allowing schnibble double-count
hypotheses.description: `unlock()` decrements `lockedToken.quantity` and zeroes `remainder`, but leaves `lastLockTime` and `unlockTime` untouched. Because `AccountManager._harvest` computes schnibbles from `lastHarvestDate` (not `lastLockTime`), the stale lock metadata is mostly benign, but `getLockedWeightedValue` still reads `quantity` so the weighted value drops correctly. The real issue is that after a partial unlock, `unlockTime` remains in the past, so the user can immediately unlock the rest without re-locking, and `setLockDuration` will accept a shorter duration because `lastLockTime + _duration < unlockTime` check uses the stale `lastLockTime`. This lets a user repeatedly reset their lock duration downward while keeping the same `lastLockTime`, gaming the lock-bonus calculation in `BonusManager._calculateLockBonus` which uses `playerSettings.lockDuration` (updated) but the on-chain lock state is inconsistent.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Lock tokens with max duration to accrue high `lockDuration`. 2) Wait until unlockTime passes. 3) Call `unlock` for a tiny quantity — `lastLockTime` stays old, `unlockTime` stays old. 4) Call `setLockDuration` with a small duration; the check `lastLockTime + _duration < unlockTime` fails only if new duration is smaller than the (already elapsed) old unlockTime, which it isn't since unlockTime is in the past. 5) `playerSettings.lockDuration` is now small, but `BonusManager.getHarvestBonus` reads `_settings.lockDuration` — so the user can flip between high and low lock bonuses at will while keeping tokens locked.
hypotheses.impact: Users can manipulate their lock-duration bonus arbitrarily, inflating harvest schnibbles and thus claim share in ClaimManager periods.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `unlock()`, when `lockedToken.quantity == 0`, reset `lastLockTime` and `unlockTime` to 0; and in `setLockDuration`, base the check on `block.timestamp` rather than stale `lastLockTime`.

hypotheses.title: LockManager._lock lets migrationManager bypass remainder/NFT accounting
hypotheses.description: Inside `_lock`, the block that computes `remainder` and `numberNFTs` and calls `nftOverlord.addReveal` is guarded by `if (msg.sender != address(migrationManager))`. This means when MigrationManager calls `lockOnBehalf`, no reveal NFTs are minted and `lockedToken.remainder` is not updated. However, `lockedToken.quantity += _quantity` still runs, and `lockedToken.unlockTime` is reset to `block.timestamp + _lockDuration`. A user can therefore use the migration path to extend their lock duration on already-locked tokens without triggering the normal remainder accounting, and the `remainder` from prior locks is silently dropped (since `quantity = _quantity + lockedToken.remainder` is computed but `lockedToken.remainder` is never reassigned in the migration branch).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker locks a small amount to build up a `remainder`. 2) Attacker migrates via `lockFundsForAllMigration` / `migrateAllNFTs`, which calls `lockOnBehalf` from MigrationManager. 3) The migration branch skips `lockedToken.remainder = remainder`, so the old remainder is added into `quantity` but never persisted — the attacker's effective locked quantity is inflated by the stale remainder on the next lock, and the unlockTime is reset without NFT reveal accounting.
hypotheses.impact: Inconsistent locked quantity accounting; users can inflate effective locked value (and thus `getLockedWeightedValue` → plots, harvest bonus) without corresponding NFT reveals.
hypotheses.recommendation: Always update `lockedToken.remainder` and `lockedToken.quantity` consistently; only skip the `nftOverlord.addReveal` call for migration, not the remainder bookkeeping.

hypotheses.title: Migration lockFundsForAllMigration allows double-lock via discriminator bypass
hypotheses.description: The check `if (_userLockedAction[msg.sender] != UserLockedChoice.NONE) revert` guards against re-locking, but `_userLockedAction` is also written by `burnNFTs`/`burnRemainingPurchasedNFTs` (setting LOCKED_BURN). Meanwhile `setUserLockedAction` (localAdmin) can flip it back. More importantly, `_userClaimedOnce[msg.sender] = true` is set without checking previous state, and `_userLockedAmounts[msg.sender].totalLockedAmount` is not zeroed, meaning a user who locks funds and then has their tokenIds list not cleared can be walked through migrateAllNFTs repeatedly without the LOCKED_FULL_MIGRATION marker preventing re-deposit if the marker is later reset by burn flows. The combination of `_userLockedAction` and `_userClaimedOnce` being set independently means refund/claim status can desync from actual deposits.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User calls lockFundsForAllMigration (locks funds, marker set to LOCKED_FULL_MIGRATION). 2) If marker is later overwritten (e.g., burn path) while tokens still map to unclaimed snapshots, user calls lockFundsForAllMigration again, depositing more funds against the same snapshots that were never marked claimed because migrateAllNFTs re-uses tokens across calls when `_skip` sliding window overlaps. 3) Additional deposits extracted via migrateAllNFTs locking boost.
hypotheses.impact: Double-counted migration amounts feeding lockManager.lockOnBehalf, inflating locked balances and locked-weighted value used for daily schnibbles and plot counts; potential insolvency of rewards.
hypotheses.recommendation: Make `_userClaimedOnce` check the sole source of truth for "has locked", zero out `_userLockedAmounts` on lock, and forbid re-entry into lockFundsForAllMigration regardless of `_userLockedAction`.

hypotheses.title: migratePurchasedNFTs charges user before reentry check on _userPurchasedAction
hypotheses.description: The function sets `_userPurchasedAction[msg.sender]` only indirectly (not at all in the shown code — only checks it is NONE). Since nothing writes a terminal value in this function, a user can call `migratePurchasedNFTs` repeatedly with the same tokenIds. On repeat calls, claimed snapshots are `continue`-skipped and `quantity` stays 0, but the check `if (msg.value != (quantity * discountFactor) / 10e12)` then requires msg.value == 0 — fine for a user calling with 0 wei. So each call migrates zero tokens, but a race window exists where between a burned-set and the migrate call, `snapshot.claimed` can be flipped for entries that still owe payment. Also `_migrateNFTs` mints new NFTs and calls `lockOnBehalf`, which requires the user to be registered — a mismatch between purchased-path users and lock-eligibility can revert mid-state after `snapshot.claimed = true` (already set inside `_migrateNFTs`).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls migratePurchasedNFTs with a valid signed list. 2) Inside `_migrateNFTs`, some snapshots are marked claimed. 3) `lockOnBehalf` reverts (user not registered / subaccount). 4) Whole tx reverts (state rolls back) — but any partial call that does succeed can leave claimed/pending states mismatched against payment because `_userPurchasedAction` is never flipped to a terminal choice, allowing another attempt against partially-migrated state.
hypotheses.impact: NFTs burned while migration lock never completed; user loses original NFT and receives no new mint / locked boost.
hypotheses.recommendation: Set `_userPurchasedAction[msg.sender] = UserLockedChoice.LOCKED_FULL_MIGRATION` (or terminal) at the start of migratePurchasedNFTs and verify lock preconditions before mutating snapshots.

hypotheses.title: LandManager._farmPlots landlord schnibbles not deducted from renter total
hypotheses.description: `schnibblesTotal` is computed, then `schnibblesLandlord = (schnibblesTotal * latestTaxRate) / 1e18`, and the renter receives `schnibblesTotal - schnibblesLandlord` while the landlord receives `schnibblesLandlord`. This is correct in isolation, but `latestTaxRate` is read from `_toiler.latestTaxRate` which is only updated on stake/transfer/farm. If the landlord changes their tax rate via `updateTaxRate`, existing toilers keep the old rate until they next farm — that is documented. The real accounting bug is that `schnibblesTotal` is computed from `(timestamp - _toiler.lastToilDate) * BASE_SCHNIBBLE_RATE` and then adjusted by `finalBonus` which can be negative (down to -20%). When `finalBonus` is negative enough, `schnibblesTotal` can underflow the `int256` cast or produce a value smaller than `schnibblesLandlord`, causing `schnibblesTotal - schnibblesLandlord` to underflow and revert, or (if it doesn't revert) the landlord receives more than the total generated.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker stakes an NFT with a realm/rarity combination that yields a large negative `finalBonus` (e.g. -20%). 2) Waits a long time without farming. 3) Calls `farmPlots`; `schnibblesTotal` after bonus is small, but `schnibblesLandlord` is computed from the post-bonus value, so the subtraction is safe. However, if `finalBonus` is applied to a very small `schnibblesTotal`, rounding can make `schnibblesLandlord > schnibblesTotal`, causing underflow revert and locking the user's farm.
hypotheses.impact: Farm function reverts, locking rewards; or landlord receives more than generated, draining the schnibble pool.
hypotheses.recommendation: Clamp `schnibblesLandlord` to `schnibblesTotal` and ensure `finalBonus` cannot make the total negative.

hypotheses.title: Migration discountFactor applied without bounds allows zero or inflated lock
hypotheses.description: `discountFactor` is read from config with no bounds check and is used as `(totalLockAmount * discountFactor) / 10e12`. If `discountFactor` is set to 0, all migrations lock 0 tokens (users lose their locked value entirely). If set very high, users lock far more than intended, diluting other players' plots and harvest rewards. There is no per-user or per-token cap.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not directly attacker-triggerable without config change, but any user who migrates while `discountFactor` is misconfigured suffers; a griefer who can influence config (via compromised admin) can drain value from all migrators.
hypotheses.impact: Migrators lock 0 tokens (loss of locked value) or lock inflated amounts (dilution of other players' rewards).
hypotheses.recommendation: Enforce `discountFactor` within a sane range (e.g., 1e12 to 10e12) at config load and revert migrations if out of range.

hypotheses.title: MigrationManager._migrateNFTs calls lockOnBehalf during iteration
hypotheses.description: In `_migrateNFTs`, the loop mints new NFTs via `_nftOverlord.mintForMigration`, burns old ones, and finally calls `_lockManager.lockOnBehalf`. The function has `nonReentrant` on the public entries `migrateAllNFTs` and `migratePurchasedNFTs`, but the internal `_migrateNFTs` is invoked by both. The lockManager call to `lockOnBehalf` triggers `_lock` which calls `nftOverlord.addReveal` and does a `safeTransferFrom`. Critically, `snapshot.claimed = true` is set before the NFT calls, so state is protected.
hypotheses.attackPath: no reentry path into _migrateNFTs due to snapshot.claimed flag; malformed or reentrant lockManager could double-mint only if new snapshots appear.
hypotheses.impact: Low - protected by claimed flag and nonReentrant.
hypotheses.recommendation: Already covered by nonReentrant and claimed flag. No action strictly needed.

hypotheses.title: MigrationManager.migratePurchasedNFTs allows re-migration via duplicate tokenIds
hypotheses.description: `migratePurchasedNFTs` iterates over the caller-supplied `tokenIds` array and accumulates `quantity += purchasedUnlockPrice` for each unclaimed snapshot. However, it does not deduplicate the input array. If the same tokenId appears multiple times, the loop will count it multiple times for `quantity` (the `snapshot.claimed` check only prevents double-counting after `_migrateNFTs` marks it claimed, but the quantity accumulation happens before `_migrateNFTs` is called). The attacker pays `(quantity * discountFactor) / 10e12` but `_migrateNFTs` will only migrate the unique tokens, so the attacker overpays — or, if the check ordering is exploited, the attacker can cause accounting mismatches.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `migratePurchasedNFTs([id, id, id])` with the same purchased tokenId repeated. 2) The loop accumulates `quantity = 3 * purchasedUnlockPrice`. 3) `_migrateNFTs` is called with the array; it marks the snapshot claimed on the first iteration and skips subsequent duplicates. 4) Attacker pays 3x the required amount for 1 NFT, or if the contract logic is reversed, gets credit for multiple migrations.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect payment accounting; attacker can overpay (loss of funds) or, if combined with other logic, cause inconsistent state between paid amount and migrated NFTs.
hypotheses.recommendation: Deduplicate `tokenIds` before accumulating `quantity`, or accumulate quantity inside `_migrateNFTs` based on actually-migrated snapshots.

hypotheses.title: burnNFTs / burnRemainingPurchasedNFTs re-process already claimed snapshots
hypotheses.description: Both burn functions iterate `for (uint256 i = _skip; i < maxLength; i++)` and use `if (snapshot.lockAmount == 0 || snapshot.claimed) continue;` — however, if the caller passes successive `_skip` values that overlap (e.g., skip=0 then skip=0 again after the list shift, or skip=0 and skip=3), already-claimed entries are skipped, but any entries beyond SKIP_AMOUNT that were never reached can be re-burned by choosing a smaller `_skip` after a larger one. There is no monotonic cursor per user; the `_skip` is supplied by msg.sender and only compared to list bounds, not to the previously processed offset.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls burnNFTs(self, 5), burning tokens 5-9, marking those snapshots claimed, earning points. 2) Attacker later calls burnNFTs(self, 0): unprocessed tokens 0-4 are burned normally, but no enforcement prevents reprocessing positions already covered by a prior call if the list length changed. Because `migrateAllNFTs` uses the same array, a mismatch between burning and migrating can leave some claimed snapshots eligible to be counted as purchases.
hypotheses.impact: Points awarded twice for the same rarity bucket in edge cases; also possible to convert locked-NFT snapshots into purchased category accounting, mispricing.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track a per-user burned offset and enforce `_skip >= lastProcessedOffset`, or remove `_skip` entirely and process deterministically.

hypotheses.title: LandManager.farmPlots writing landlord metadata during renter loop
hypotheses.description: In the loop over staked tokens, the code calls `accountManager.updatePlayer(landlord, landlordMetadata)` inside the loop, and `accountManager.updatePlayer(mainAccount, renterMetadata)` at the end. But `_getMainAccountRequireRegistered(landlord)` is called at the top of each iteration to reload `landlordMetadata`. Repeatedly calling updatePlayer inside the loop is an external call through the AccountManager - which itself checks `onlyConfiguredContract3`. The key issue: if `landlord == mainAccount` (impossible due to CantStakeToSelfError) or if the landlord is another renter's account, the initial `landlordMetadata` read is stale for a landlord who holds multiple staked munchables of other renters.
hypotheses.attackPath: Player A rents plots to landlords B and C. Within one `farmPlots()` call from A, the loop reads landlord B's unfedSchnibbles fresh; but if the same landlord appears twice, accounting is still per-iteration fresh due to re-read. This is more an accounting concern than direct exploit.
hypotheses.impact: Potential missed or double-counted schnibbles for landlords with multiple renters in the same call.
hypotheses.recommendation: Aggregate landlord schnibbles in a local mapping and update once per landlord after the loop.

hypotheses.title: fundTreasuryDistributor trusts caller's token bag contents
hypotheses.description: `receiveTokens` is `onlyConfiguredContract(StorageKey.RewardsManager)` — good — but the function blindly iterates `tb` and does `IERC20(tokenContract).transferFrom(msg.sender, _treasury, amount)` for each entry. When the configured RewardsManager calls it, the msg.sender is RewardsManager, so the ERC20 `approve` calls in RewardsManager's `_forwardYield` are the ones spending. This is fine in isolation, but the trusted call path opens a concern: if `_treasury` is misconfigured (or the distributor is re-used/reconfigured by the config owner to point to an arbitrary token), transfers can pull any token the RewardsManager approved. That specific concern is owner-config. More importantly, for the untrusted caller path, this contract's protection rests entirely on `RewardsManager` calling it; there is no protection to stop tokens listed to refer to arbitrary contracts if the RewardsManager's upstream calls are ever wrong. This is over-narrow as an untrusted-caller vuln — the only direct issue is the missing validation that `tb[i].tokenContract` is a configured token.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not directly reachable by untrusted external actors because of `onlyConfiguredContract(RewardsManager)`. Requires a second bug to exploit; therefore not a standalone finding.
hypotheses.recommendation: Validate that tokens being forwarded are the expected USDB/WETH/ETH.

hypotheses.title: LockManager.unlock reentrancy via forceHarvest and token callback
hypotheses.description: The `unlock` function follows Checks-Effects-Interactions ordering but the initial `accountManager.forceHarvest(msg.sender)` is an external call that happens before the `lockedToken.quantity -= _quantity` state update. forceHarvest internally can call `_harvest` and `landManager.updatePlotMetadata` which callback into other contracts. Additionally the ERC20 `token.transfer` uses safeTransfer-less direct transfer that could be a hook token. However, the function is guarded by `nonReentrant` which mitigates direct reentry to unlock.
hypotheses.attackPath: N/A - nonReentrant guard prevents this via direct reentry into unlock. However cross-function reentrancy is still possible since only same-function calls are blocked.
hypotheses.impact: Potential for cross-function reentrancy - but the primary functions lock() and unlock() both have nonReentrant. Would only be exploitable if multiple functions were entered.
hypotheses.recommendation: Move forceHarvest after state updates, and use SafeERC20.safeTransfer for all token transfers.

hypotheses.title: PrimordialManager.hatchPrimordialToMunchable state updated before external mint
hypotheses.description: The function sets `primordials[_caller].hatched = true;` before calling `nftOverlord.mintFromPrimordial(_caller)`. While this ordering is actually the correct CEI pattern, the current code does not have a reentrancy guard. mintFromPrimordial externally calls into rngProxy which stores requests. However, there is no nonReentrant modifier on this function, and if the `hatched` flag was moved or if other state (like a double-check) were added later, this could be reentered. Note however that the hatched flag check prevents reentry into the same path.
hypotheses.attackPath: N/A - reads the hatched flag before proceeding, so no direct exploit.
hypotheses.impact: Theoretical - no direct exploit path with current code.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add nonReentrant guard for defense in depth.

hypotheses.title: SnuggeryManager.exportMunchable transfers NFT before state cleanup
hypotheses.description: The function calls `erc721Token.transferFrom(address(this), _caller, _tokenId)` before removing the token from the `snuggeries` array. If the NFT contract uses ERC721Receiver hooks (MunchNFT uses standard ERC721 which does not implement onERC721Received on transferFrom), the receiver's callback could reenter. More importantly, the `chonkUpdated` modifier runs `claimManager.forceClaimPoints` before the function body, and `_recalculateChonks` after. But between transfer and removal, the token is still recorded as being in the snuggery while the owner has changed.
hypotheses.attackPath: If MunchNFT were modified to support ERC721Receiver callbacks (or another hook), the receiver could reenter exportMunchable and pull the same tokenId into a snafu. With current MunchNFT this is not exploitable.
hypotheses.impact: Theoretical - potential double-removal or index corruption if reentered.
hypotheses.recommendation: Remove state before calling transferFrom, and add nonReentrant.
